name: Mausi (मौसी), about 55, chapter 1 voice

voice.register: Hindi-first; the loudest and fastest voice in the cast, warm and bossy like a front-room tuition teacher with her Class 3. She talks in bursts: two to four bubbles of short closed sentences, most ending on ! or ?, the first bubble starting over the end of yours. Her shape: she says a word twice to push the room along ('Chalo, chalo!', 'Na, na!'), asks a question and answers it herself before anyone can, and tags a statement 'hai na?' and moves on before anyone replies. A triple is kept for a peak, at most once a scene, and 'Suno, suno, suno!' is the one the family quotes back. Her long run is a string of short loud sentences, never a comma chain (Mama ji's run-on) and never a list (Mummy's jobs, Mami's statuses). The common fillers come and go in her lines as in anyone's (arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas, theek hai); what marks her is the shape and the classroom and kitchen her words come from, never a word she owns. Pace quick and rising. When cross she gets louder and faster, the only one in the family who does; when moved she goes silent, the only time she does. No numbers at all, not even ordinals. One shout bubble a chapter at most (rule 35, which is 1.09), and never a whisper, because she cannot whisper. Each bubble is at most 10 words (rule 62), so a longer thought becomes more bubbles. She is never the asker (rule 37) and never reacts to who was picked (rule 39).
voice.mix: A Hindi frame with single English words in it, the older speakers' pattern in the realism notes (1.1). Her English carries feeling and school, not trade: sorry, tension, first class, topper, homework, copy (exercise book), class, teacher, fail, late mark; in chapter 1 also the travel nouns berth and chart. The everyday English verb with kar or ho comes to her as it does to any schoolteacher, with school verbs: 'top kiya', 'check karo', 'fail ho gayi', 'pass ho gaya' (of you only as a command, since a past said of you would mark a gender). Mummy is told apart by what she turns into counter English, not by owning the pattern. She never switches a whole clause into English (Mama ji's and Mami's way). Her Hindi is everyday small-town Hindustani with a teacher's words in it (inaam, bujho, copiyan, 'kaan pakdo', 'khaali pet'), and the town's ordinary words fikr, waqt and zaroor come to her plainly too; never spelled to sound funny. The tag 'hai na?' is a habit of hers, not a word she owns; in English mode it becomes the Indian English 'right?'. In Hinglish mode she reads as Roman Hindi with those English words (how a Hinglish bubble looks waits on rulebook Q6). A Hindi-first reader reads every line aloud (rule 65).
tics: Says a word twice to hurry, refuse or soothe, the way real Hindi does: 'Chalo, chalo!', 'Na, na!', 'Aao, aao.', 'Sorry, sorry!', or a name twice ('Munna, Munna!', 'Bhabhi, Bhabhi!'); to elders 'Chaliye, chaliye!'. The triple is saved for a peak, at most once a scene: 'Suno, suno, suno!' to call the room (the one the family quotes back), or 'Na, na, na!' at news she will not have. 'Haay' is never doubled or tripled, because हाय-हाय is a lament and a protest chant.

Asks a question and answers it herself, like the riddle-setter she is every morning, blurting the answer before anyone can guess: 'Kiski? Hamari!', 'Main padosan hoon? Nahin!', 'Andhera? Koi baat nahin!', 'Chai ya halwa? Halwa!'. The one question in the year she cannot answer herself is 'Kisne karwaayi?' at the lower berth, and then she goes silent.
Ends a statement with 'hai na?' and is gone before anyone answers; in English mode, 'right?'. Not on every line: a few a scene at most.
Quotes people back word for word: 'Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha…'. Her memory is exact; she never misquotes.
Says what she feels, out loud, to the whole room: love ('Bahut yaad aayi'), hurt ('Amma pehle Chhoti ko bulaati hain!'), sorry. Silent only when moved, palm to her chest.

Runs the room like her class: marks the late ('Late mark!'), sets the classroom's punishment in fun ('Kaan pakdo!', to Munna or Tinku), grades a favour ('Ekdum first class!', at most once a chapter), now and then fails herself when she is wrong ('Aaj teacher fail!'), and measures a loss by her pupils ('meri class ka inaam'). Her teaching is in her mouth, not only in one wordless picture, so she is more than the loud aunt who feeds. But the classroom is one of her two sources, never her stamp: about one line in four reaches for it at most, and the kitchen and her exact memory of what people said carry the rest (the flood is 'Achaar ke martbaan upar!', not her pupils' exercise books; being wrong is 'Galat kaun nikla? Main!').
Worries in quick questions about the body and the belly, and answers for you if you are slow: 'Kuch khaya bhi? Nahin?', 'Chot toh nahin lagi?'.

Food as punctuation: 'Pehle khao' (the only 'Pehle' that is hers; 'Pehle ___' as a courtesy is yours), 'Khaali pet baat nahin!', 'Muh meetha karo!', and something held out as she says it, her face in the frame. 'Haay' never comes just before she holds out food.
Report-card verdicts on habits, never on character, in all her judging notes ('Never sits still for long.').
'Hamara, hamari' (ours) for anyone she is proud of ('hamari topper'), but never of you, since it would mark your gender.
She always has an answer and almost never says 'pata nahin', which is why 'Kisne karwaayi?' silences her.
When cross: louder and faster, hand on hip, the basket bag set down hard, and her own catchphrase fails ('Koi sunta bhi hai? Nahin!').
catchphrases: 'Suno, suno, suno!' | 'सुनो, सुनो, सुनो!' | 'Listen, listen, listen!' (her opener and the line people quote back; her one regular triple. Anyone may say 'suno' or 'chalo'; the tripled call to the room is hers)
'Maine kaha tha na?' | 'मैंने कहा था न?' | 'Didn't I tell you?' (whenever something she predicted comes true, good news above all)

'Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha…' | 'पिछले साल तुमने कहा था…' | 'Last year you said…' (the quote-back; it marks no gender, because with तुमने the verb agrees with what was said; you are the doer, though, so it waits on the owner's rule 66 question in address 0). None of the three has a number in it.
voice.exclamation: 'Haay!' | 'हाय!' | English mode 'Haay!' too, the way Mami keeps 'Ish'. Spelled short, the way the cry sounds in a Hindi-belt town, not the film spelling 'Haaye' that makes her the screen's Punjabi aunty. For sympathy, surprise and delight, and just before she says a feeling ('Haay! Bahut yaad aayi.'). At most once a scene, and never just before she holds out food. Nobody else in the cast uses it. It has no religious meaning on its own; the guard is that it is never followed by a name of any kind or by 'Maa': no 'Hai Ram', 'Haay Ram', 'Haay Rabba', 'Haay Allah', 'Haay Maa', 'Ui Maa'. Never doubled or tripled (हाय-हाय is a lament and a protest chant). Keeping it in English mode also ends the old mix-up of her 'Oh!' with Mama ji's 'Oho!'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain and doubled, food held out as she says it, her face in the frame: 'Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao.' | 'सॉरी, सॉरी! पहले खाओ।' | 'Sorry, sorry! Eat first.' To an elder: 'Sorry, sorry! Pehle khaiye.' Tinku and you now say a plain 'sorry' too; hers is told apart by the double and the food, not by owning the word. Wrong in front of everyone, she says so first and loudest, her own question answered at once: 'Galat kaun nikla? Main! Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao!'; now and then she fails herself as a teacher instead ('Aaj teacher fail, hai na?'). THANKS, GIVEN: plain words, out loud, to the whole room: 'Bahut achha laga!' | 'बहुत अच्छा लगा!' | 'So nice of you!' ('Bahut achha kiya.' is Mummy's thanks, so the sisters' words differ, and with लगा you are not the doer); and her teacher's grade 'Ekdum first class!' | 'एकदम फ़र्स्ट क्लास!' | 'First class!' at most once a chapter, so the grade stays a treat and never turns into a code. 'Thank you' is not her habit at home, as it is not for most of her generation; she says it to a stranger like anyone. WHEN SHE IS THANKED: she wants it heard: 'Achha? Zor se kaho! Amma bhi sunein!' | 'अच्छा? ज़ोर से कहो! अम्मा भी सुनें!' | 'Really? Say it louder! Let Amma hear too!' Only Amma's thanks, in December, makes her silent. LOVE: said out loud, to the whole room: 'Haay! Bahut yaad aayi.' | 'हाय! बहुत याद आई।' | 'Haay! I missed you so much.' At a parting, the same key: 'Abhi se yaad aa rahi hai!' | 'अभी से याद आ रही है!' | 'Missing you already!' Mama ji's love is warm and one to one, with a hug; hers is loud and to the room, with food.

arre, achha, haan, dekho, bas, theek hai | अरे, अच्छा, हाँ, देखो, बस, ठीक है | everyone's fillers, in the middle of her lines like anyone's ('arre' only as a filler: as an exclamation on its own it is Captain sahab's, matrix 2.15, and hers is 'Haay')
berth, chart | बर्थ, चार्ट | chapter 1's travel nouns, the same in every mode
never: Any doubt of a report of being followed or harassed, or of a dowry demand: no 'sach mein?', 'pakka?', 'galatfehmi', 'misunderstanding', 'imagined', 'chhodo', 'jaane do', 'hota rehta hai' about it. She is the first to believe, and the hard topic never reaches a bubble or a story panel anyway (rule 26); she has no line in the lead-in or settle of a hard decision. Her 'Na, na!' and 'Ye nahin chalega!' are for harmless news only.

Any religious word or exclamation (rule 3): no Hai Ram, Haay Ram, Haay Rabba, Bhagwan, Allah, Rab, Wahe Guru, Ishwar, Jesus, tauba, 'shukr hai', 'Ui Maa', 'Mata ji' as a goddess; in English mode no Gosh, Golly, Goodness, Oh my, Heavens, Lord, Thank God. No caste word, no brand.
Any number in speech: no figures, no counts, no years (rule 2), no ordinals ('teesri class' is struck), no 'ek-ek', 'teen baar' or 'sau mein sau'. 'First class' stays as an idiom of praise.

Any word that gives you a gender: beta, bachcha, bhaiya, didi, raja, rani; 'hamara/hamari' of you; any verb or adjective that agrees with you: kitne/kitni bade/badi ho gaye, aa gaye/aa gayi, thak gaye/gayi, -oge/-ogi, khaate/khaati raho (rules 8 and 66). 'How grown up you've got' becomes 'Chehre pe thakaan.'

Other people's set phrases, so the blind sort can tell her apart. These are phrases, not fillers: arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas and theek hai are everyone's. Kept out (an exclamation here is barred only as her habitual cry; the word itself stays free): 'Arre waah' and 'Arre!' as an exclamation on its own (Captain sahab's, matrix 2.15; hers is 'Haay!'), 'Ek-ek karke' and 'Pehle ___' as a courtesy (yours; she keeps only 'Pehle khao'), 'Lo. Aadha.' and a one-word 'Theek.' bubble (Mausa ji's), 'aur haan' as a joiner, 'Oho!', 'full' and a one-word 'Roz.' (Mama ji's), 'Kamaal' and 'Reached?' (Papa's), 'Had hai!', 'Ye mere hisaab mein' and 'Iska bill nahin' (Mummy's), 'Gazab!' and the 'haan?' tag (Tinku's), 'Not out', 'Next ball', 'Well played' (Captain sahab's), 'Baap re', a closing 'Bas.', 'Chai piyo', 'Main yahin hoon', 'Khush raho' (Nani's), 'Uff' and 'Jeete raho' (Masterji's), 'Hain?', 'Mazboot', 'Galti hui', 'Ho jayega' (Mausa ji's), 'Ish', 'Tick', 'Correct?', 'pending', 'Congratulations' (Mami's), 'Badhiya' as a one-word verdict and 'Shukriya' (yours), 'Badhai ho' (Mummy's, if the owner allows it), and 'Mubarak ho' (unused for now: it and 'Badhai ho' are both everyday congratulations and take one ruling, and an Urdu-speaking reader checks that both sides are treated alike, India verdict 3).
A whole English clause (Mama ji's and Mami's way): her English stays single words, and school verbs with kar or ho.
A comma chain or a list: her long run is short closed sentences, never Mama ji's run-on or Mummy's and Mami's lists.

Character words or verdicts on anyone: aalsi, kaamchor, raub, besharam, badchalan, chalu; nothing on anyone's morals, marriage or dress; no sentence about ladkiyan, ladke, aurtein or mard in general (rule 22). Her talk is energy and care, never gossip about people.
The stock aunty's questions to you: shaadi, rishta (a match), salary or 'kitna kamate', weight, looks, skin colour (gori, kaali, saanwli) for anyone, 'naukri kab'.
A joke at her own body or age, or at her loudness as mockery: she laughs first and the strip laughs with her ('Meri class aise hi sunti hai'), never at her.
Film lines or famous catchphrases (rule 3): never 'Main hoon na'.
A second shout in a chapter; any whisper (rule 35).
More than one triple in a scene, or 'Haay' more than once in a scene or just before she holds out food.

Any card person's name, or any word from a decision's card notes, in a bubble before or during that decision, in either language (rule 36). In chapter 1 that rules out, until the decision that carries them: phone, tea, water, blanket, trip, 'last', bag, sari, tiffin, food (खाना), coach (डिब्बा), seat, window, family, everyone (सबके), पास, साथ, बार, तरह, joke, bus (and बस), platform, town (शहर), maths, coaching, teaches, and बोल. The test-set lines below are not panel lines; any line placed in a panel re-runs the build's note-word check.
address: To you: तुम, only in commands ('Ab batao', 'Idhar baitho', 'Pehle khao', 'Jaldi aana'), 'who should' asks, and lines where you are not the doer ('Chehre pe thakaan', 'Bahut yaad aayi', 'Tumhari khabar'); no address word, or her opening 'Suno, suno, suno!'. The first time in a chapter she names Mummy to you she says 'tumhari Mummy' | 'तुम्हारी मम्मी', and 'Chhoti' after that, since 'Chhoti' alone is opaque to a new reader (Nani's note). Never beta (rulebook Q7 is open, and it stays out until then), bachcha, bhaiya, didi. Lines rule 66's checker flags where you are not the doer, which a native reader clears: आई (agrees with याद), लगी (with चोट), लगा (her thanks 'बहुत अच्छा लगा!', with मुझे understood), मुझे (a pronoun). OWNER QUESTION (rule 66): in some of her lines you are the doer of a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing done and so marks no gender: 'Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha' (catchphrase 2, sample 5), 'Kuch khaya bhi?' (sample 8), 'khana khaya??' (typing 1) and 'Parathe rakhe, hai na?' (test moment 6). Rule 66 allows तुम in only three shapes (commands, 'who should' asks, lines where you are not the doer), and this is none of them. Either the owner adds 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' to rule 66 as a fourth shape, or the native reader clears each line and the build puts it on its cleared list. No wording changes if the owner agrees. The same question covers Tinku's, Papa's, Mummy's and Mama ji's lines of this shape.

To Nani: 'Amma', आप and -इए ('Amma, bujhiye kaun?', 'Pehle khaiye'). Never 'Ammi' or 'Mataji' (the house says 'Amma'; realism 1.3, and an Urdu-speaking reader checks that both sides are treated alike, India verdict 3).
To Mummy: 'Chhoti', तुम. In English mode, 'your Mummy' when she speaks of her to you.
To Papa: no address word, आप ('Chaliye, chaliye!', 'Jaldi kijiye!'); to you, 'tumhare Papa'. Never 'Tinku ke Papa' (a wife's way of naming her own husband).
To Mama ji: 'Munna', तुम (his childhood pet name; readers confirm).

To Mausa ji: 'Aji' | 'अजी', with आप ('Abhi khaiye!'), since a wife who calls her husband 'Aji' says आप to him. The note asks for आप from him to her too; his file now has तुम both ways and no word for her, so the readers settle it in the one family address table. READERS' QUESTION: 'Aji' with आप is real, but it can sound like the 1970s film wife; many small-town teachers of her age say 'Suniye' | 'सुनिए' or no word at all. If the Hindi-first readers hear the film in it, her lines to him take 'Suniye' or no address word, still with आप, and nothing else changes, since her shape marks her without it.
To Masterji and Captain sahab: their titles and आप.
To strangers: 'Bhaiya' to the stall man, 'Sahab' to the ticket checker, आप; neither is ever a card person.

What they call her: Nani 'Badi' (तुम); Mummy and Papa 'Didi' (आप); Mama ji and Mami 'Badi Didi' (आप); Tinku and you 'Mausi' (आप, with -इए); Mausa ji no word ('tumhari Mausi' to you); Masterji 'Behenji' (आप), what a neighbour of about sixty says to a schoolteacher of about fifty-five; Captain sahab and her old pupils 'Madam ji'. All for readers to confirm (rule 65), in the one family address table.

Bahut yaad aayi.' | Hindi 'हाय! बहुत याद आई।' (kept, rings true; gender-free: आई agrees with याद, which rule 66 check 3 flags and a native reader clears)

Bade wale upar! Jaldi kijiye!' | Hindi 'चलिए, चलिए! बड़े वाले ऊपर! जल्दी कीजिए!' (चलो to a jija reads as a step down, so चलिए; doubled, not tripled)

Why?' / 'Am I a neighbour? No! Now tell me. Directly.' | Hinglish 'Suno, suno, suno! Tumhari khabar, tumhari Mummy se? Kyon?' / 'Main padosan hoon? Nahin! Ab batao. Seedha mujhe.' | Hindi 'सुनो, सुनो, सुनो! तुम्हारी ख़बर, तुम्हारी मम्मी से? क्यों?' / 'मैं पड़ोसन हूँ? नहीं! अब बताओ। सीधा मुझे।' (the scene's one triple; 'tumhari Mummy' because it is the first time she names Mummy to you, and 'Chhoti' from here on; your line plus her two bubbles make three pieces of text, at most 20 counted words (rule 62); तुम्हारी agrees with ख़बर; पड़ोसन हूँ is her own gender and मुझे is a pronoun, both flagged and cleared by a native reader; no note word (phone, साथ, सबके, पास, बोल, platform, शहर))

Hai na?' | Hindi 'अम्मा पहले छोटी को बुलाती हैं! है न?' (kept; 'hai na?' invites a denial nobody gives; 'pehle' here is a complaint, not your 'Pehle ___' courtesy)

WORRYING (about you, loud, answering for you): English 'You look so tired! Eaten anything? No? Eat first!' | Hinglish 'Chehre pe thakaan! Kuch khaya bhi? Nahin? Pehle khao!' | Hindi 'चेहरे पे थकान! कुछ खाया भी? नहीं? पहले खाओ!' (kept, rings true; the opening 'Haaye' is dropped, since she holds out food at the end; gender-free: थकान is the subject, खाया follows कुछ, and खाओ is a command; you are the doer of खाया, so it waits on the owner's rule 66 question (address 0))

(a school verb with kar; no score, since scores are Tinku's; 'hamari' marks Tinku, a woman, and is never used of you)

Kisne karwaayi?' | Hindi 'नीचे की बर्थ? मेरे लिए? किसने करवाई?' (the one question in the year she cannot answer herself; Papa, from behind, answers (his writer owns that line); then her one silent panel of the chapter, palm to her chest)

(two bubbles of short closed sentences, never a comma chain)

PARTING (to you, at the carriage door as the train is about to go): English 'Missing you already! Come back soon. Definitely!' | Hinglish 'Abhi se yaad aa rahi hai! Jaldi aana. Zaroor!' | Hindi 'अभी से याद आ रही है! जल्दी आना। ज़रूर!' (रही agrees with याद and आना is the infinitive command, so neither marks a gender, though rule 66's checker flags both; 'zaroor' is the town's word, not one man's)
DECEMBER (Nani's kitchen, after Nani thanks her first): no line. Her one silent panel of the year, palm pressed to her chest, mouth shut.

habits: Device: a big-screen Android phone in a plain flip case with no markings (rule 3). She reads it held a hand's width from her nose, since she is short-sighted and wears no glasses; that distance is her phone trait (six files share 'font at its largest', so it is not). Painted blank; every word on it is live text (rule 30).

Mostly voice notes, long ones, the phone held flat under her chin like a plate and spoken at full volume so the whole room hears. They open 'Haan suno....' and close '....chalo, khana kha lena 😊'. On screen a voice note is a live-text card: a play mark, a long bar and her first words, with no length figure, so no number reaches her lines.
When she types: Roman Hinglish, all lowercase except 'OK', spelled the way she says it ('haay', not 'haaye') and always in full, never short forms like 'h' or 'k' (Masterji's and Tinku's).

Punctuation: four dots '....' between every phrase instead of full stops or commas; double question marks '??', which are hers (Mama ji keeps '!!'). One long message, never a burst of short ones (Mama ji's), never one item a line (Papa's), never a list (Mami's); the one exception waits on the owner, if message cards are held to the 10-word cap (habit 9). She types her doubles too, with no commas ('jaldi jaldi', 'abhi abhi'), the one triple the family quotes ('suno suno suno'), and her self-answered question ('kaun jeeta?? hamari topper').
No figures, even typed: no times, no counts, no prices. Her daily send is a riddle, not a sum.

Emoji: 😊 at the end of nearly everything, even bad news (the family knows to read past it); 😋 for food. Never 👍 (Mummy's), never a person emoji (it carries a gender and a skin tone), and 🙏 not at all until the owner decides (realism 2.2).

Her one daily send is her own: 'aaj ki paheli' (today's riddle), a traditional children's riddle in words to the family group early each morning, whose answers she marks by voice note at night. Never a good-morning flower (Papa's), never gods, politics, a famous face, false news or a home remedy (rule 3; realism 2.2).
Timing: replies within seconds all day, answers a one-word message with a long voice note, and is sending from four in the morning. No reply means she is cooking.
Typos: autocorrect turns her Hinglish into English words and she sends it anyway; it is never shown as a joke on her.

The family group is mentioned, never shown (owner, 23 Oct). A message reaches the player as one message card. OWNER QUESTION (rule 62): the rulebook does not yet say whether a message card counts as a spoken line, with the 10-word cap, or as sign words. Four of her messages are over 10 words (samples 0, 3, 5 and 7). If the cap applies, each splits at her '....' into cards of 10 words or fewer, written out in that sample's note; no message changes until the owner answers. Split, every card still ends on her '....', '??' or 😊, so it never reads as Mama ji's burst of short '!!' messages.

How others' typing meets hers: Mummy answers 'ok 👍' within a minute in shop hours and never after nine; Papa replies with one full-stopped sentence; Tinku replies 'mausi 😂'; Mausa ji sits beside her and does not need to.
samples: To you, the evening before the train (a message card on the painted blank phone): 'suno suno suno....kal raat wali train....tum bhi saath ho na?? apni baatein seedha mujhe batana....tumhari mummy se nahi 😊' (listen listen listen....tomorrow night's train....you're with us, right?? tell me your news yourself....not through your Mummy). Gender-free: 'saath ho' and a command; 'tumhari mummy' because it is the first time she names her to you. If it is shown in chapter 1 it is a sign, so the note-word check applies (साथ). If the owner holds message cards to the 10-word cap (habit 9), it goes as three cards: 'suno suno suno....kal raat wali train....' / 'tum bhi saath ho na??' / 'apni baatein seedha mujhe batana....tumhari mummy se nahi 😊'.

To you, after any trip: 'khana khaya?? kya kya khaya?? 😋' (eaten?? what did you eat??). Kept, rings true. About food only: 'Reached?' is Papa's. Gender-free: खाया follows खाना; you are the doer, so it waits on the owner's rule 66 question (voice, address 0).
Voice note to you before dawn, a live-text card: '▶ Haan suno.... neend nahi aayi....toh socha....' (Yes, listen.... couldn't sleep....so I thought....). No length figure on the card.

Family group, early morning (mentioned, or shown as a single card): 'aaj ki paheli....ek thaal moti se bhara, sabke sir par aundha dhara....kya hai?? jawab shaam tak....tinku tum mat batana 😊' (today's riddle....a plate full of pearls, held upside down over everyone's head....what is it?? answers by evening....Tinku, don't you answer). Kept, rings true. The answer is the night sky; a traditional children's riddle, where 'ek' is the article 'a', not a count. If the owner holds message cards to the 10-word cap (habit 9), it goes as three cards, the riddle whole on the middle one: 'aaj ki paheli....' / 'ek thaal moti se bhara, sabke sir par aundha dhara....' / 'kya hai?? jawab shaam tak....tinku tum mat batana 😊'.
To Mausa ji at night: 'aji....bp ki goli ka waqt....abhi khaiye 😊' (aji....time for your BP pill....take it now). आप, as in her speech to him.

To Mummy before dawn on the ward night, from Nani's house: 'chhoti....amma se baat hui....unko bhi neend nahi....fikr mat karo....subah aati hoon....tum so jao 😊' (Chhoti....spoke to Amma....she can't sleep either....don't worry....I'll come in the morning....you go to sleep). Mummy, who never messages after nine, reads it in the morning. If the owner holds message cards to the 10-word cap (habit 9), it goes as two cards: 'chhoti....amma se baat hui....unko bhi neend nahi....' / 'fikr mat karo....subah aati hoon....tum so jao 😊'.

To you, after your good news: 'haay....maine kaha tha na?? ekdum first class....mithai kab?? 😋' (haay....didn't I tell you?? first class....when are the sweets??). Gender-free: no verb agrees with you.

To Mummy, her hurt typed and then smiled over: 'amma ne aaj bhi pehle tumhe bulaaya....koi baat nahi....main toh hoon hi 😊' (Amma called you first again today....never mind....I'm always here anyway). The 😊 is why nobody hears it. If the owner holds message cards to the 10-word cap (habit 9), it goes as two cards: 'amma ne aaj bhi pehle tumhe bulaaya....' / 'koi baat nahi....main toh hoon hi 😊'.

changed: Triples cut back to doubles by default ('Chalo, chalo!', 'Na, na!', 'Aao, aao.', 'Sorry, sorry!', 'Munna, Munna!'), the way real Hindi repeats a word; a triple is kept for a peak, at most once a scene, and 'Suno, suno, suno!' stays the one the family quotes back. The test set now opens with a triple twice in twelve (moments 3 and 8, and 8 is a line the readers marked true) instead of eight times. Why: the real-India note, too many triples.

'Haaye' is now spelled 'Haay' in Roman letters (हाय is unchanged) and kept in English mode too, replacing 'Oh!'. It comes at most once a scene and never just before she holds out food, so the worry line and the good-news line lose it. Why: 'Haaye' is the film spelling of the Punjabi aunty, the very type the comics review named; keeping 'Haay' in English also ends the blur with Mama ji's 'Oho!'.

'Aji' now goes with आप: 'Aji, goli khaayi? Nahin? Haay! Abhi khaiye!', the typed 'abhi khaiye', and moment 4 with no तुम command ('Mujhe phiki chahiye.'). Why: a wife who calls her husband 'Aji' says आप to him. Mausa ji's file still has तुम both ways, which the note wants matched, so the family address table settles it.
The order to Papa and Mausa ji is now 'Chaliye, chaliye! Bade wale upar! Jaldi kijiye!'. Why: the Hindi note, चलो to a jija reads as a step down.

English tags are now 'right?' across her English lines ('Amma calls your Mummy first! Right?'), and 'Didn't I say so?' is now 'Didn't I tell you?', 'Absolutely first class' is now 'First class!', 'No tension!' is now 'Don't take tension!', and 'copybooks' is now 'notebooks'. Why: Indian English says 'right?' or 'na?', and the English-mode readers heard the rest as translated.

Common fillers are no longer banned for her: she says 'Achha?' (moment 7), 'arre' may come mid-line as anyone's filler (as an exclamation it stays Captain sahab's, matrix 2.15), and the never list now keeps out only other people's set phrases. The bans on arre, dekho, achha, bas, theek, chalo/suno as anyone else's, 'please', 'pata nahin', 'mausam' and 'barsaat' are gone ('pakka?' stays out only as doubt after a report). Why: cast-wide note 1. Fillers belong to everyone, and she is told apart by shape and word sources.

The English verb with kar or ho is now hers when it suits a schoolteacher: 'Phir se top kiya, hai na?', and 'check karo', 'fail ho gayi' in her uses. She still never switches a whole clause. Why: cast-wide note 2. It is the most common Hinglish pattern, and Mummy is marked by her counter English, not by owning the pattern.

Sorry and thanks are plain words. Sorry is 'Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao.', and since Tinku and you now say a plain 'sorry' too, hers is told apart by the double and the food. Thanks is now the everyday 'Bahut achha kiya!' (since mended to 'Bahut achha laga!', so that 'Bahut achha kiya' is Mummy's alone), with the teacher's grade 'Ekdum first class!' at most once a chapter. Why: cast-wide note 3, no thanks or sorry in a code more than once a chapter.

The town's words reach her plainly: 'fikr mat karo' to Chhoti, 'goli ka waqt' to Aji, and 'Jaldi aana. Zaroor!' in a new parting sample. Why: cast-wide note 8, so fikr, waqt and zaroor are not one tailor's badge.

Moment 2 drops the cold food ('Khana thanda!') for 'Ab aaye ho? Late mark! Kaan pakdo!', the classroom's own punishment said in fun. Moment 11 now worries ('Koi baat nahin! Chot toh nahin lagi?') instead of a second class joke. Why: cast-wide note 6, where five people reached for cold food in moment 2; the change also keeps her school words from becoming a gimmick.

The first time she names Mummy to you in a chapter, she says 'tumhari Mummy' and then 'Chhoti' ('Tumhari khabar, tumhari Mummy se? Kyon?'; the typed 'tumhari mummy se nahi'). Why: Nani's note, 'Chhoti' alone is opaque to the player-reader.

Lines get more of their verbs ('Abhi se yaad aa rahi hai!', 'Bachche aaj bhi tumhari benchon par baithte hain!'), and the shout ends 'Ye nahin chalega!' instead of 'Kabhi nahin!'. Why: cast-wide note 9 on verbless telegrams, and 'Kabhi nahin!' did not answer her own question the way a Hindi-belt aunt would.

Moment 3 keeps her own congratulation ('Naukri lag gayi! Maine kaha tha na?', now 'lag gayi' as it is said); 'Badhai ho' is left for Mummy if the owner allows it, and 'Mubarak ho' unused. Why: cast-wide note 4.

Kept word for word, as the readers marked true: 'Bahut yaad aayi'; 'Rishta main laayi thi. Berth bhi main laaun?'; 'Kaisi hoon? Batati hoon! Ghutna dukhta hai, dil nahin!'; 'Chehre pe thakaan! Kuch khaya bhi?'; 'Na, na, na! Band? Toh meri class ka inaam?'; 'Late mark!'; 'Ekdum first class!'; the riddle 'ek thaal moti se bhara'; the '....' typing with 😊; 'khana khaya?? kya kya khaya??'. Also kept: her essence, want, fear, contradiction, year arc, the shout's place, the lower-berth silence, the December silence, every never-rule on harassment and dowry reports, and the note-word limits.

Open points for readers and the owner: whether Mausa ji says आप back to her (his file says तुम); whether 'Meri class aise hi sunti hai' and 'Kaan pakdo!' to a grown brother sound right to a Hindi-first reader; whether 'Badhai ho' is allowed (owner); rule 66's fourth shape and rule 62 for message cards (owner, the entries below); whether 'Aji' sounds like the film wife (readers, the entry below).

Moment 9 is now 'Gali mein nadi? Haay! Achaar ke martbaan upar! Chalo, chalo!' | 'गली में नदी? हाय! अचार के मर्तबान ऊपर! चलो, चलो!' | 'Lane's a river? Haay! Pickles up! Come on, come on!'. Why: the Hindi note, where 'Arre' worked as an exclamation, which matrix 2.15 gives to Captain sahab, so her own 'Haay' takes its place; and the real-India note, where the classroom had become her stamp, so the flood reaches for the courtyard's pickle jars instead of her pupils' exercise books.

Moment 5 is now 'Galat kaun nikla? Main! Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao!' | 'ग़लत कौन निकला? मैं! सॉरी, सॉरी! पहले खाओ!' | 'Who got it wrong? Me! Sorry, sorry! Eat first!'. Why: the same real-India note; it was the third school line of four in the test set. Now two of twelve reach for school ('Late mark! Kaan pakdo!' and 'meri class ka inaam', both marked true and kept), and the rest come from the kitchen, her questions answered at once and her exact memory. 'Aaj teacher fail' stays a now-and-then habit (tic 5, sorry), and tic 5 now says the classroom is one of her two sources, never her stamp.

Rule 66: address 0 now sets out the owner's question on pasts with ने where you are the doer ('Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha', 'Kuch khaya bhi?', 'khana khaya??', 'Parathe rakhe, hai na?', and, until her thanks became 'Bahut achha laga!', 'Bahut achha kiya!' said to you): add it to rule 66 as a fourth shape, or have the native reader clear each line onto the build's cleared list. The lines' notes point there, and the cleared list now holds only lines where you are not the doer. No wording changed. Why: the Hindi note, rule 66 names only three shapes for तुम and the file had cleared these as 'a ने past', which the rule does not name.

Rule 62 and typed messages: typing habit 9 now asks the owner whether a message card is held to the 10-word cap, and samples 0, 3, 5 and 7 carry their split at her '....' into cards of 10 words or fewer, ready if the cap applies. No message changed. Why: the Hindi note, four of her messages run to between 13 and 20 words.

Masterji's word for her stays 'Behenji' (आप), and address 10 now says why and that Masterji's file, which has 'Mausi ji', is to be matched to it. Why: the two address tables disagreed, and 'Behenji' is what a neighbour of about sixty says to a schoolteacher of about fifty-five.

'Aji' now carries a readers' question (address 6, uses 28): if the Hindi-first readers hear the 1970s film wife in it, her lines to Mausa ji take 'Suniye' or no address word, still with आप. Why: the real-India note.
